purpose: Ultrasound-guided pleural fluid drainage — site selection, needle technique staying above the rib, and the re-expansion pulmonary edema risk with large-volume drainage.
entryPrompt: Ultrasound guidance is standard of care wherever available — it meaningfully lowers the pneumothorax rate compared to the blind landmark technique.

nodes.body: Diagnostic: a new or unexplained pleural effusion, to send fluid for Light's Criteria and further studies. Therapeutic: symptomatic relief of dyspnea from a large effusion. Use ultrasound to confirm a fluid pocket large enough and accessible enough to tap safely, and to identify the diaphragm/liver/spleen position — ultrasound guidance meaningfully lowers the pneumothorax rate compared to the classic blind landmark technique and is the standard of care wherever available.

Patient sitting upright, leaning forward over a bedside table if tolerated — this pools the effusion posteroinferiorly. Typical entry site is the posterior axillary line, one or two interspaces below the top of the effusion as marked by ultrasound, generally not below the 8th-9th intercostal space to avoid the diaphragm/abdominal organs.

nodes.prompt: 3. Needle technique — above the rib, not below
nodes.body: Enter just ABOVE the superior border of the rib below the chosen interspace — the neurovascular bundle (intercostal artery, vein, nerve) runs along the INFERIOR margin of each rib, so walking the needle onto the top of the lower rib and then just over it avoids it. Infiltrate local anesthetic down to and including the pleura (this is often the most painful step if under-anesthetized). Advance under continuous aspiration or continuous ultrasound visualization until fluid returns; many kits use a catheter-over-needle technique to reduce lung-puncture risk once fluid is reached.

For therapeutic drainage, a common practice limit is roughly 1.5 L in one sitting — beyond this, the risk of re-expansion pulmonary edema rises, particularly with rapid drainage of a large, long-standing effusion. Stop drainage (regardless of volume) if the patient develops chest pain, cough, or dyspnea during the procedure — these can signal the lung re-expanding faster than it tolerates, or an evolving pneumothorax.

A post-procedure chest X-ray to assess for pneumothorax is traditional but not mandatory in a low-risk, asymptomatic, ultrasound-guided tap with a single easy pass — reserve it for multiple needle passes, air aspirated during the procedure, new symptoms, or a patient who will need mechanical ventilation shortly after (where even a small pneumothorax matters more). Send pleural fluid promptly for Light's Criteria plus any further studies (cell count/differential, glucose, pH, cytology, culture) indicated by the clinical question.

checklist: Ultrasound used to confirm the fluid pocket and mark site/depth immediately before prepping
Entry above the rib, not below — neurovascular bundle avoided
Local anesthetic carried down to the pleura, not just the skin
Volume drained monitored, generally capped near 1.5 L, stopped early for new symptoms
Fluid sent for Light's Criteria plus further studies as indicated
